strengths: PAPE addresses an important practical problem: estimating deployed classifier performance when production labels are unavailable or delayed. Combining density-ratio weighting with score calibration is a simple, potentially useful approach.

Under covariate shift, adequate support overlap, and correct target calibration, the conditional-expectation argument provides a sound basis for estimating accuracy and confusion-matrix probabilities.

The evaluation is substantial within Folktables: 959 dataset-model combinations and 36,557 production chunks across five tasks and five model families. PAPE achieves the best aggregate results in all six Table 1 comparisons. Comparisons against both unweighted calibration and direct importance weighting help establish the value of the combination.

Public datasets, a code-repository link, and explicit chronological splits support reproducibility. The discussion candidly acknowledges concept shift, support mismatch, and sampling uncertainty. No material research-ethics concern is apparent in the reported study.
weaknesses: The central claim of supporting any performance metric is not established. Equations (1)–(2) apply to additive per-example utilities, whereas F1 is a nonlinear ratio and AUROC is pairwise. Corresponding estimators and derivations are missing. For example, an always-positive classifier with prevalence 1/2 has population F1 of 2/3, but averaging singleton F1 through Equation (1) gives 1/2 even with perfect calibration. This affects two of the three headline metrics. Equation (4) also incorrectly equates expected absolute label residual with absolute conditional-mean residual; these differ even under perfect calibration.

The practical estimator is insufficiently specified in the manuscript. The density-ratio classifier and weighted calibrator architectures, fitting objectives, hyperparameters, preprocessing, and weight stabilization are not described. Algorithm 1 estimates density ratios on the classifier's training observations without explaining overfitting controls. The repository link is valuable, but these choices are central to interpreting and reproducing the reported gains.

The evaluation's numerical scale exceeds its demonstrated diversity: all cases originate from related US Census datasets. Year-to-year changes need not satisfy invariant label conditionals, so these experiments do not isolate performance under covariate shift. Controlled shifts with known density ratios, calibration diagnostics, and broader datasets would strengthen the mechanism and generality claims. The sample-size analysis covers only one selected case.

The statistical support for superiority needs clearer reporting. The Wilcoxon result is given as p = 0.0 without identifying the testing unit or accounting for dependence among chunks and models sharing data. Confidence intervals and case-level effect distributions are absent. Chunk-weighted, reference-SE-normalized aggregates can also obscure practical error magnitudes and favor larger datasets; raw errors and aggregation by dataset would help assess the relatively modest accuracy and AUROC gains over IW.

The methodological originality is not sufficiently distinguished from existing importance weighting and calibration methods. The main theoretical argument combines conditional expectation with an established reweighting identity. The paper offers neither a characterization of when weighted calibration improves over direct IW nor experiments that isolate the relevant bias–variance tradeoff. The empirical improvement is promising, but the additional scientific insight remains limited.

Several presentation claims need narrowing. The abstract says the method relies only on predictions and probability estimates, although density-ratio estimation requires reference and production features. Its statement that no assumptions about the shift are needed obscures the essential covariate-shift and overlap requirements. Figures 1–2 also label the proposed method 'M-CBPE' without explaining its relationship to PAPE.
